tagline: Galleries, a website and a client CRM under one login.
verdictSummary: Pixieset sells the whole photographer's back office in one place, and each piece on its own is ordinary software — which makes this a kinda. The reason people pay is that the pieces know about each other: a booking becomes a gallery becomes an invoice without retyping. A personal build can have that too, and the honest gap is the print store and the mobile apps, plus the ordinary cost of running your own delivery.
coreLoopDIY: Wire the pieces together rather than rebuilding each: a booking creates the gallery shell, the gallery notifies the client, and delivery closes the job — one client record all the way through.
whatYouLose: the print store and its fulfilment
the mobile apps for you and the client
the hosted website builder with its templates
email campaign sending included in the plan
hosted reliability on gallery delivery day
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is four tools and a spreadsheet, and every seam between them is a place a wedding gets forgotten. Eight dollars for one login is a rational trade for a one-person business.
prompt:
Build a photographer's back office where one client record runs from enquiry to delivery, and prove there is no retyping.

Stack: your choice, Postgres, object storage, Docker Compose, a domain with TLS, and a transactional email provider.

One Client record: name, contacts, notes. Everything else attaches to it.

The pipeline, as one flow rather than four features:
1. **Enquiry** from a public form on your site, creating the Client and a Job with a date and a type.
2. **Booking**: the Job gains a contract (a Markdown template rendered with client fields, signed by typed name plus a stored timestamp, IP and a copy of the exact text signed — the last part is what makes it worth anything later) and a deposit recorded manually.
3. **Shoot day**: a checklist from a template by job type.
4. **Delivery**: creating the gallery from the Job pre-fills the title, date and client, and sending it emails the client from a template with their name and the gallery link. The gallery's existence is visible on the Job.
5. **Close**: final payment recorded, files archived to cold storage, and a review request sent after N days.

The test that proves the design: from enquiry to close, the client's name and email are typed exactly once. Write it as an end-to-end test.

Gallery: unguessable URL, password or personal link, responsive images, favourites with a target count, per-photo comments, zip download at a set resolution.

A dashboard that is a work list, not statistics: jobs by stage, anything overdue at its stage, unpaid balances, and galleries expiring this month.

A public site: a few pages and portfolio galleries from the same photo store, server-rendered, no client framework.

Write tests for the single-entry-of-client-details flow, for contract signing storing the exact rendered text, and for cold-storage archiving with one-command restore.

Do not build a print store or payment processing — link to whatever you already use.

faq.q: Why store the exact contract text at signing?
faq.a: Because a template changes, and a signature that points at "the current template" proves nothing. Storing the rendered text, the typed name, the timestamp and the IP is the minimum that makes a click-signed contract worth having.

faq.q: Is the no-retyping test not trivial?
faq.a: It is trivial to write and it is the whole design. Most self-built photographer tools are four separate apps by month three, and the end-to-end test is what stops that happening.

faq.q: Why a work list instead of a dashboard?
faq.a: Because a one-person business needs to know what to do today, not what its conversion rate was last quarter. Jobs stuck at a stage and unpaid balances are actionable; charts are not.

faq.q: What does Pixieset actually charge for?
faq.a: Storage tiers and email campaign volume, with Studio Manager and the editing suite billed separately from about $12 a month each. The entry tier is 10 GB, which a single wedding can fill.
